complete.problem: Explain how a puddle on the playground disappears on a sunny day.

steps.text: The Sun heats the water in the puddle.
steps.annotation: The Sun is the energy source that drives the water cycle.

steps.text: The liquid water gains heat and evaporates, changing into water vapour.
steps.annotation: Evaporation is the change from liquid water to invisible water vapour, and it happens faster when the water is warmer.

steps.text: The water vapour rises and mixes with the air, so the puddle shrinks until it is gone.
steps.annotation: The water has not vanished - it has moved into the air as vapour, ready to condense again elsewhere.

complete.selfExplanation: Explain where the puddle water has gone, using the word evaporate.

faded.problem: Explain how rain forms after water evaporates from the sea.

steps.text: Water evaporates from the sea and rises as water vapour.
steps.annotation: Heat from the Sun drives evaporation from the sea surface.

steps.text: High up, the air is colder, so the water vapour cools and condenses into tiny liquid droplets.
steps.annotation: Condensation is the change from water vapour back to liquid water, and it happens when vapour cools.

steps.text: The droplets gather into clouds, grow heavier, and fall as rain.
steps.annotation: When the droplets are too heavy to stay in the air, gravity pulls them down as precipitation.

faded.selfExplanation: The first step is shown. Predict the next change of state and what causes it.

paired.problem: Explain why wet clothes dry faster on a windy day than on a still day.
paired.solution: Water evaporates from the clothes into the air. On a windy day the moving air carries the water vapour away from the clothes, so the air next to the fabric stays dry and more liquid water can keep evaporating. On a still day the air near the clothes becomes damp, so evaporation slows down.
